newsitem.title: USA: House, Senate edging toward each other on tax bill.
newsitem.headline: House, Senate edging toward each other on tax bill.

text.p: Senate and House tax negotiators made progress on Thursday in their efforts to merge two tax-cut bills into one but major issues remained unresolved.
The Senate side of the bargaining table issued its first counteroffer in which it accepted one of the airline-related revenue raising provisions in the House bill.

The Senate offered to go along with the House plan to charge a $15.50 per passenger international arrival and departure fee, with the caveat of keeping current law for domestic flights to and from Alaska and Hawaii. Currently there is an international departure fee of $6 per passenger.

The fee increase was added to the House bill during debate in the House Ways and Means Committee to replace a proposed tax on Indian tribal gaming that lawmakers balked at and removed from the legislation.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, has repeatedly said the proposed international arrival and departure fee was too high and should be brought down to $10 per passenger as he had originally proposed.

The Senate and House have so far stuck to their guns on the major issues -- the $500 per-child tax credit, higher education incentives, expansion of Individual Retirement Accounts, estate tax relief and a capital gains tax cut.
The group of lawmakers is trying to iron out differences in the Senate and House tax-cut legislation so that one final bill can go before the full Congress for a vote.
The tax conferees also have to deal with White House objections to provisions in both bills because ultimately President Clinton will have to sign off on the legislation.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, said he hoped Congress would reach agreement with Clinton on tax and budget legislation "very shortly."
But some Democrats have questioned whether agreement can be reached that quickly on some of the stickier issues.

The legislation would implement the May budget agreement reached between congressional leaders and the White House aimed at wiping out the deficit over five years and giving an $85 billion net tax cut.
House tax negotiators met Thursday afternoon to go over the Senate proposal and planned to issue a rebuttal offer soon, a House Republican aide said.

"We've been clearing out the underbrush," the aide said. As smaller issues are resolved, the decision-making on major items was likely to involve just the main hitters such as Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, Archer, and administration officials, the aide said.

Among the issues needing resolution is a 20-cents per pack tax increase on cigarettes which is in the Senate bill but not in the House version. House Republicans have said many members oppose that tax increase.

The Senate offer showed agreement on some small areas such as a reduction in the tax rate on apple cider having an alcohol content of no more than seven percent to 22.6 cents per gallon, the same as for beer produced by small breweries. Currently cider is taxed at the same rate as wine of $1.07 per gallon.
